title: Object literals
description: Object literals — shorthand properties, computed keys, method shorthand, and dot vs bracket access.

notes: Dot access requires a literal identifier; bracket access takes any expression.
Computed keys [expr] run at object-creation time; the result is coerced to a string (or Symbol).
Method shorthand defines a normal function — `this` refers to the object when called as obj.method().

questions.q: What does `{ name }` expand to when name is a variable holding "Ada"?
questions.explain: Shorthand expands to `{ name: name }` — the key is the identifier's text, the value is whatever that variable currently holds.

questions.q: Given `const k = "x"`, which literal sets key "x" to 1?
questions.explain: Only the brackets evaluate `k`. `{ k: 1 }` and `{ "k": 1 }` both take the identifier literally and produce the key `"k"`, not `"x"`.

questions.q: When MUST you use bracket access instead of dot?
options: Never — they are interchangeable; dot is just less typing
When the key is in a variable or not a valid identifier
When the value is a function — bracket access binds `this` correctly
When the object was created with Object.create(null) — dot fails on prototype-less objects
questions.explain: Dot needs a literal identifier after it, so `user.k` looks up the key `"k"` and never the value of `k`; bracket takes any expression and coerces the result to a string. Dot works fine on `Object.create(null)` objects.

options: A getter — accessing `obj.greet` would invoke the body
greet: function greet() { ... } — the shorthand adds a name binding inside the function
questions.explain: Shorthand defines an ordinary non-arrow function, so `this` is the receiver at call time — that's why `makeUser("Ada", 36).greet()` can read `this.name` and an arrow could not. It sets `.name` but, unlike a named function expression, adds no self-reference binding inside the body.
